title: “THEY THAT WAIT UPON THE LORD SHALL RENEW THEIR STRENGTH” — YOU MAY HAVE MISUNDERSTOOD WHAT GOD MEANT BY “WAIT”
paragraphs: “THEY THAT WAIT UPON THE LORD SHALL RENEW THEIR STRENGTH” — YOU MAY HAVE MISUNDERSTOOD WHAT GOD MEANT BY “WAIT”
Biblical waiting is not sitting still while your life falls apart. Sometimes the waiting room is the very place where God is rebuilding the person who will eventually walk through the door.
There is a kind of tired that sleep cannot fix.
You know it if you have ever stared at the ceiling after midnight while everyone else seemed to be sleeping peacefully.
Your body was lying down.
But your mind was running.
You prayed.
You waited.
You tried to believe.
Then you prayed again.
And somewhere between the unanswered prayer and another disappointing morning, a question slipped into your heart that you were almost afraid to say aloud:
“God… have You forgotten me?”
Maybe you have been waiting for healing.
Waiting for work.
Waiting for your marriage to change.
Waiting for your child to come back to God.
Waiting for a door to open.
Waiting for the financial pressure to break.
Waiting for freedom from something you have fought privately for years.
Waiting for the grief to become bearable.
Waiting for an answer.
Waiting for direction.
Waiting for God to do something—anything—that proves this painful chapter is not the end of your story.
And perhaps the hardest part is not simply that you are waiting.
It is watching other people move while you remain where you are.
Someone else gets the opportunity.
Someone else announces the pregnancy.
Someone else gets married.
Someone else's ministry grows.
Someone else's prayer appears to be answered.
Someone else posts the testimony you desperately wanted to be yours.
You congratulate them.
You press the heart button.
You tell them, “Praise God.”
And you mean it.
Mostly.
Then you put down the phone, stare into the silence, and whisper something Christians sometimes feel ashamed to admit:
“Lord… when will it be my turn?”
If that sentence has ever lived inside you, Isaiah 40 was written closer to your pain than you may realize.
Because before Isaiah gives us the soaring eagle, he gives us an exhausted people.
Before the promise comes the complaint.
Israel says:
“My way is hid from the LORD, and my judgment is passed over from my God.”
That is Isaiah 40:27.
In other words:
God does not see what is happening to me.
God has overlooked my case.
God has forgotten where I am.
Sound familiar?
Then comes God's answer.
Not an explanation of every delay.
Not a timetable.
Not a date circled on a calendar.
God gives them something greater.
He gives them a revelation of Himself.
The everlasting God does not grow tired.
The Creator has not lost control.
His understanding has not reached its limit.
And the God who never runs out of strength gives strength to people who have none left.
Then Isaiah arrives at one of the most beloved promises in Scripture:
“וְקוֹיֵ יְהוָה יַחֲלִיפוּ כֹחַ”
Ve-qovei YHWH yachalifu koach.
“But they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength…”
—Isaiah 40:31
The Hebrew matters.
The word translated “wait” comes from קָוָה — qavah.
It carries the sense of waiting, looking for, hoping, expecting.
That changes something.
Biblical waiting is not spiritual laziness.
It is not folding your arms and saying, “Well, I guess God will handle everything.”
It is not refusing responsibility.
It is not abandoning obedience.
It is not doing nothing.
Biblical waiting is living in active dependence upon God when you cannot yet see what God is doing.
It is obedience without visible results.
Prayer without immediate answers.
Faithfulness without applause.
Hope without evidence you can hold in your hands.
It is planting when the ground still looks empty.
It is obeying God today while trusting Him with tomorrow.
That is why waiting can hurt so much.
Because real waiting requires surrender.
And surrender means admitting something our flesh hates admitting:
“I cannot control this.”
You cannot force somebody to love you.
You cannot manufacture God's timing.
You cannot manipulate a prodigal home.
You cannot command tomorrow to arrive today.
You cannot bully a closed door into becoming God's will.
You cannot hurry God.
And sometimes what feels like God withholding something from you is actually God removing your illusion that you were ever in control.
That hurts.
But it can also become holy ground.
Because some of the deepest work God performs in us happens while nothing appears to be happening around us.
Think about Joseph.
He had a dream before he had a prison.
God showed him something about his future, and then Joseph's circumstances seemed to move in precisely the opposite direction.
Betrayed.
Sold.
Falsely accused.
Imprisoned.
Forgotten by a man he had helped.
If Joseph had judged God's faithfulness only by his immediate circumstances, he could have concluded that the dream had died.
But the prison was not the conclusion.
God was still writing.
Think about David.
Anointed as king… then chased through the wilderness.
There was oil on his head while there was still a cave over his head.
Promise did not eliminate process.
David had opportunities to seize what God had promised through sinful means, yet waiting required him to refuse shortcuts.
That is one of the great tests of waiting:
Will you still want God's promise if receiving it requires God's way?
Because desperation can make counterfeits look like answered prayers.
Loneliness can make the wrong relationship look providential.
Financial pressure can make dishonest money look like provision.
Ambition can make compromise look like opportunity.
Impatience can convince you that because God has not moved quickly, you are permitted to move without Him.
But faith says:
I would rather wait with God than arrive somewhere God never sent me.
Maybe somebody reading this needs that sentence tonight.
Do not destroy tomorrow because today feels unbearable.
Do not trade obedience for relief.
Do not call something God's answer merely because it ended your waiting.
Not every open door was opened by God.
Not every opportunity deserves your yes.
Not every relationship is worth keeping.
Not every shortcut leads toward the promise.
Sometimes faith looks less like soaring and more like refusing to leave the place where God told you to stand.
And Isaiah's promise becomes even more beautiful when you notice its progression.
“They shall mount up with wings as eagles…”
Wonderful.
“They shall run, and not be weary…”
Powerful.
“They shall walk, and not faint.”
Walk?
After soaring?
After running?
Why finish with walking?
Perhaps because most of the Christian life is lived there.
Not every day feels like an eagle day.
Not every morning feels supernatural.
Sometimes there is no dramatic breakthrough.
No emotional worship moment.
No miraculous phone call.
No sudden answer.
You simply get out of bed.
You pray again.
You open your Bible again.
You forgive again.
You resist temptation again.
You go to work again.
You care for your children again.
You choose honesty again.
You refuse bitterness again.
You repent again.
You trust again.
You take one more step.
And heaven calls that faithfulness.
We celebrate soaring because everyone can see it.
God also sees walking.
Especially when walking costs you everything.
Maybe you are not soaring right now.
Maybe you are barely walking.
Do not despise the walk.
The promise includes you too.
“They shall walk, and not faint.”
Notice also what Isaiah does not say.
He does not say those who wait upon the Lord will never become tired.
Verse 30 has already admitted that even youths become weary and young men stumble.
Human strength has limits.
Your exhaustion does not automatically mean you have failed God.
Sometimes you are exhausted because you have been carrying something heavy for a very long time.
The promise is not that Christians become emotionally indestructible.
The promise points us away from self-sufficiency toward the inexhaustible God.
“יַחֲלִיפוּ כֹחַ — yachalifu koach.”
They will renew their strength.
The strength you need does not have to originate in you.
That is good news for the person who has reached the terrifying sentence:
“I don't think I have anything left.”
Maybe you don't.
But God does.
And perhaps that is exactly where grace becomes more than religious vocabulary.
The Gospel itself confronts our obsession with saving ourselves.
We could not climb our way back to God.
We could not outwork our sin.
We could not perform ourselves into righteousness.
We could not wash away our guilt.
So Jesus Christ came to us.
The sinless Son of God entered our broken world.
He bore sin at the cross.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose again.
Christianity is not ultimately the story of exhausted human beings finally becoming strong enough to reach God.
It is the story of God coming down to rescue people who could never rescue themselves.
That is grace.
And perhaps there is another kind of waiting happening right now.
Maybe God has been waiting on you.
You have been asking Him to change your circumstances while He has been exposing your heart.
You want the door opened.
He wants the sin surrendered.
You want relief.
He wants repentance.
You want Him to remove the consequences while you keep protecting the compromise.
You want a new chapter without letting Jesus rewrite the old one.
There are things waiting cannot heal if what God is calling for is repentance.
There are moments when “waiting on God” becomes a spiritual phrase we use to postpone obedience.
If God has already told you to forgive, you do not need another sign.
If Scripture has already called something sin, you do not need another confirmation.
If you know you need to repent, tomorrow is not more holy than today.
Grace is not permission to keep hiding.
Grace is God's invitation to come out of hiding.
Bring Him the addiction.
Bring Him the secret messages.
Bring Him the pride.
Bring Him the bitterness.
Bring Him the pornography.
Bring Him the jealousy.
Bring Him the dishonest money.
Bring Him the affair.
Bring Him the anger.
Bring Him the religious performance.
Bring Him the thing you keep deleting from your history but cannot delete from your conscience.
Jesus already knows.
And still He calls sinners to Himself.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
It is God calling you home.
The cross means your scandal does not have to become your final identity.
Peter denied Jesus.
Thomas doubted.
Paul persecuted Christians.
The thief beside Jesus had no lifetime left to repair his reputation.
Yet grace entered their stories.
That does not make sin insignificant.
It makes Christ magnificent.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe your waiting season has exposed things you did not know were inside you.
Jealousy.
Fear.
Control.
Anger at God.
Envy of other people's blessings.
A dependence on people's approval.
A faith that was strong as long as God behaved according to your timetable.
Do not waste the exposure.
God can use waiting like a mirror.
Not to destroy you.
To show you what needs surrender.
And perhaps years from now you will realize that while you were begging God to change your situation, He was transforming you into someone who could survive the answer.
You thought nothing was happening.
But roots were growing where nobody could see them.
Character was forming.
Discernment was sharpening.
Pride was dying.
Prayer was deepening.
False dependencies were breaking.
Your theology was moving from slogans into scars.
You were learning that God is still God when the prayer is unanswered.
Still good when the door remains closed.
Still worthy when you cannot understand Him.
That kind of faith cannot be manufactured in comfort.
There are things you learn about God in the dark that daylight could never have taught you.
So if you are waiting tonight, do not confuse God's silence with God's absence.
Isaiah's exhausted people feared that their way was hidden from God.
God's response was essentially: I have not become tired. I have not stopped seeing. I have not ceased being God.
Your life is not hidden from Him.
Your tears are not invisible.
Your obedience is not wasted.
Your prayers are not meaningless because the answer has not arrived on your schedule.
Keep walking.
And when you cannot run…
walk.
When you cannot soar…
walk.
When your prayers sound beautiful…
walk.
When your prayers are only, “Jesus, help me”…
walk.
When you feel strong…
walk.
When you are trembling…
walk.
Not because walking earns God's love.
But because grace has given you somewhere to walk toward.
Jesus.
And if you fall?
Return to Jesus.
If you sin?
Repent and return to Jesus.
If you become exhausted?
Return to Jesus.
If you realize you have been running ahead of God?
Stop.
Return to Jesus.
Your hope is not ultimately in your ability to wait perfectly.
Your hope is in the One upon whom you wait.
That distinction can save an exhausted believer from despair.
Be honest.
What are you waiting for?
What has this season exposed in you?
Somebody reading beneath this article may need the evidence of God's faithfulness that your scars can provide.
Not because an algorithm deserves your attention.
You may never know whose midnight prayer meets this message because you pressed Share.
Send it privately to the believer who is exhausted.

Supporting Gospel work can be one expression of Christian generosity, but it should never be given through manipulation or compulsion. Scripture says, “Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7).
Everyone can pray.
Many can share.
Someone you know may desperately need what you nearly scrolled past.
But before you leave, remember this:
The eagle is breathtaking.
The running is inspiring.
But maybe the miracle God is giving you today is simpler.
You are still walking.
After everything that tried to break you…
you are still walking.
After prayers that seemed unanswered…
still walking.
After betrayal…
still walking.
After failure…
still walking.
After nights when you wondered whether God could possibly still want you…
still walking.
And perhaps one day you will look behind you and finally understand:
What felt like God making you wait was sometimes God teaching you that when your strength ended, His never did.
Keep your eyes on Jesus.
Your waiting room is not your grave.
And your weakest chapter does not get the final sentence when Christ is holding the pen.
